title: The Moon Cannot Be Stolen
text:
Ryokan, a Zen master and poet, lived the simplest kind of life in a little hut at the foot of a mountain. He owned almost nothing.

One evening, while Ryokan was out, a thief broke into the hut, only to find that there was nothing in it worth taking. As he was searching, Ryokan came home and caught him.

Instead of shouting for help, Ryokan spoke to him kindly. "You may have come a long way to visit me," he said, "and you should not go home empty-handed. Please take my clothes as a gift." He took off the clothes he was wearing and held them out.

The thief was bewildered. He took the clothes and slunk away into the night.

Ryokan sat down naked by his door and looked up at the moon, which was shining brightly over the mountain. "Poor fellow," he murmured. "I wish I could have given him this beautiful moon."
lesson: Meeting someone's worst moment with generosity instead of anger can unsettle them more than punishment. What matters most to you can never be taken anyway.
source: Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps, 101 Zen Stories (1919)
caveat: This is a traditional anecdote about the historical poet monk Ryokan, not a documented event.
